name: SMV tier-list threads

card.summary: Forum threads that sort physiques, facial features, surgeries or traits into ranked tiers, giving members a quick map of which improvements are widely thought to change perceived attractiveness the most.
card.aka: muscle SMV tier list, looks tier list
card.note: Tier lists are subjective community rankings, not measurements.

quick.overview:
SMV tier-list threads are posts on looksmaxxing forums in which a member ranks items (muscle groups, facial features, procedures, supplements, even ethnic groups) into S/A/B-style tiers. SMV stands for sexual market value, the community's term for overall attractiveness.

For appearance improvement, the lists work as a prioritisation shorthand: a member who sees height and frame near the top of a features list, or a particular surgery rated highly, can decide where to put effort. They are opinion posts, usually followed by replies disputing the placements; the format itself comes from video-game culture.
quick.how: Members post a list with tier headings, others reply with their own rankings or objections, and popular threads get updated versions. Topics range from muscle SMV and dimorphic features to surgeries, SARMs and anime. Readers use them as a starting point for further research rather than as measurements.
quick.risks: Lists are subjective and often disagree with each other. Some rank medical procedures or performance-enhancing compounds, and the placements reflect the poster's opinion, not clinical guidance. Some threads rank groups of people, which is contentious even within the community.

lead: SMV tier-list threads are forum posts, mainly on looksmax.org, that rank things related to attractiveness into labelled tiers. 'SMV' stands for sexual market value, a term from pick-up-artist forums that later spread through the wider manosphere and incel-adjacent spaces, where people are rated on decile or 'PSL' scales [1].

The tier-list format began in video-game communities, where players sorted characters by tournament viability; the top 'S' grade echoes Japanese grading [2]. Looksmaxxing forums borrowed it to sort anything from muscle groups to cosmetic surgeries.

For someone trying to look better, these lists serve as a prioritisation map. A 'Tier List of Dimorphic Features (Men)' thread, for example, put height and frame in the top tier, jaw and neck width next, and facial hair and hairline shape in a bottom 'doesn't matter' tier, while replies debated whether height counts as dimorphic [3]. Other threads rank plastic and cosmetic surgeries, SARMs, muscle groups and body features [4][5]. No published study validates these rankings; they record community opinion.

chain: Members rank features, muscles or procedures into tiers
Readers see which items the community thinks matter most
They choose where to spend effort on their own appearance
angle.text: The lists condense community opinion into a quick ordering of what to work on, such as muscle groups, frame, or surgeries. They are used as a starting point for deciding priorities, with the ranking itself coming from forum consensus and argument.

paras: A tier list sorts items into ordered groups, typically S, A, B, C and D, from most to least favourable. The format grew out of video-game culture, where players used it for characters and in-game elements, and has spread to films, sports teams and many other subjects, usually to prompt discussion or give a quick overview [2]. Critics of the format point out that it flattens context, a limitation noted by games journalist Maddy Myers regarding team-based games [2].

On looksmaxxing forums the same layout is applied to attractiveness. Examples include threads titled 'muscle SMV tier list', 'plastic surgery tier list', 'softmax tier list', 'updated roidmaxxing tier list for bone mass and masculinization' and a thread tier-listing SARMs with suggested stacks [4][6][7]. Others rank by race or by country, or are jokes such as theme songs [8].

One thread on male dimorphic features listed height and frame in tier 1, jaw and neck width in tier 2, chin height and browridge projection in tier 3, occipital shape and nose slope in tier 4, and facial hair and hairline shape in a lowest tier. A reply questioned whether height is dimorphic, and another answered that it is [3].

A surgery tier list graded procedures from acceptable to disliked, with the poster giving reasons for each placement; replies mostly tagged other members [9]. A SARMs thread ranked compounds by potency and selectivity and added example stacks, with the author asking readers to correct mistakes [10]. These reflect personal opinion and personal experience, not clinical recommendation.

No studies of looksmaxxing tier lists as such have been published. Researchers describing SMV note that the concept is a manosphere counterpart to the academic idea of sexual or erotic capital, and the sociological literature on that idea has been criticised for, among other things, understating cultural and social constraints on how attractiveness is valued [1].

Tier-list threads are a common way for newer members to orient themselves, and the replies often become the real content, with members disputing placements or posting their own versions. Updated versions of popular lists circulate over time, and the format is also used humorously [8].

lore.intro: Members use tier lists as shared shorthand for what matters in appearance, while regularly disputing individual placements [3][9].

claims.claim: Height and frame sit at the top of male features
claims.believers: A poster ranked height and frame in the highest tier of male dimorphic features, ahead of jaw and neck width [3].
claims.experts: No published study has tested this particular ordering; research on attractiveness examines individual traits separately.

claims.claim: Muscle can be ranked by SMV impact
claims.believers: Muscle SMV tier-list threads rank which muscle groups contribute most to perceived attractiveness [4].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined a ranking of this kind.
